title_en: Inwang jesaekdo (Scene of Inwangsan Mountain After Rain) by Jeong Seon
key_facts: Painted by Gyeomjae Jeong Seon (1676–1759) in 1751, during the Joseon dynasty, eight years before his death. An inscription dates the painting to the latter part of the intercalary fifth lunar month of that year.|Painted on paper, measuring 79.2 cm in height and 138.2 cm in width.|Designated a National Treasure of Korea on August 6, 1984.|Depicts Mount Inwang in Seoul after rainfall, with mist rising around the rocky peaks.|The painting is a representative masterpiece of late-Joseon true-view landscape painting (jingyeong sansu), which emphasized Korean landscapes observed firsthand rather than simply imitating Chinese painting conventions.|Jeong Seon lived near Mount Inwang for much of his life and moved to the foot of the mountain in 1727, becoming deeply familiar with its landscape.|Jeong Seon used repeated dark ink strokes and layers of ink to depict the massive, rain-soaked rock faces of Chimabawi. He varied the density of his brushwork to distinguish protruding rocks, shadowed valleys, and surface textures.|Unlike the conventional use of lighter ink for distant mountains, Jeong Seon rendered the distant rocky peak in dark ink. He left areas of paper unpainted to represent mist, creating a strong contrast between the rocks and the surrounding atmosphere.|The foreground contains densely clustered trees, including pine trees depicted with characteristic T-shaped forms.|The composition combines different viewpoints: buildings in the foreground appear to be viewed from above, while the mountain peaks appear to be viewed from below.|Although based on a real landscape, the painting does not reproduce every geographical detail exactly. Jeong Seon exaggerated the height of Chimabawi and may have incorporated streams associated with Suseongdong Valley and Cheongpunggye to emphasize the mountain's grandeur.|The exact reason Jeong Seon painted the work remains unknown, and art historians have proposed different interpretations.|Art historian Choe Wan-su proposed that Jeong Seon painted the work to wish for the recovery of his longtime friend, the poet Yi Byeong-yeon. In this interpretation, the clearing rain symbolizes hope for recovery. This is a scholarly interpretation, not an established fact.|Art historian Oh Ju-seok examined rainfall records in the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, which indicate that rain continued until the morning of the 25th day of the intercalary fifth lunar month in 1751. Based on these records, he proposed that Jeong Seon painted the work that afternoon. This is a scholarly hypothesis, not a confirmed date of completion.|Other interpretations suggest that the painting may have been commissioned by Yi Chun-je or created to commemorate Mount Inwang's scenery. Scholars have also proposed different identities for the house in the foreground, including a residence of Jeong Seon or a house associated with his maternal grandfather. Neither the house's identity nor its connection to the painting's purpose has been conclusively established.|The painting was donated to the National Museum of Korea in April 2021 by the family of the late Lee Kun-hee.

title_en: "Korean Traditional Wrestling" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: "Korean Traditional Wrestling" is a leaf from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do, designated as a Treasure of Korea. It is painted on paper and measures 26.9 cm in height and 22.2 cm in width.|The exact date of the album is unknown, but it is generally dated to the late 18th century.|The album currently contains 25 genre paintings, including well-known works such as Korean Traditional Wrestling and A Village School.|The album depicts everyday life in late Joseon, including work, leisure, and activities of people from various social groups.|Korean Traditional Wrestling is widely regarded as a masterpiece of Korean genre painting.|Two wrestlers compete in the center of the painting, surrounded by spectators arranged mainly in two groups in the upper and lower parts of the composition.|A toffee vendor on the left turns away from the wrestling match, contrasting with the spectators who focus on the wrestlers. The vendor also helps complete the circular composition.|Shoes placed on the ground to the right narrow the open space, visually connect the two groups of spectators, and help balance the composition.|The spectators have varied postures and facial expressions, with some leaning forward and others sitting more casually. Kim Hong-do's simple yet expressive brushstrokes convey the excitement of the wrestling match.|Rough brushstrokes convey the texture of cotton clothing, while broad, round faces and round eyes are characteristic of Kim Hong-do's genre figures.|In most paintings in the album, detailed backgrounds are omitted to emphasize the figures' postures and movements. Kim Hong-do used swift, sketch-like brushstrokes to depict lively human figures.|Kim Hong-do (1745–after 1806) was a leading painter of the Joseon dynasty who excelled in various genres, including landscape painting, bird-and-flower painting, and figure painting. He served as a court painter at the Royal Bureau of Painting (Dohwaseo) and employed a wide range of artistic styles, from refined court painting techniques to Western-influenced methods. His Album of Genre Paintings is among his representative works.|Ssireum is a traditional Korean form of wrestling in which two competitors grapple directly and use strength and technique to bring their opponent down.|Ssireum has a long history in Korea, with wrestling scenes depicted in Goguryeo tomb murals, including those in the Ssireum Tomb and Jangcheon Tomb No. 1.|During the Joseon dynasty, ssireum was enjoyed by people from a wide range of social backgrounds, from the yangban elite to ordinary commoners. This does not establish the social status of individual figures in Kim Hong-do's painting.|Ssireum became a seasonal folk custom associated with traditional Korean holidays such as Dano, Baekjung, and Chuseok. The painting itself does not establish which occasion, if any, is depicted.

title_en: "A Village School" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: "A Village School" is a leaf from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do, designated as a Treasure of Korea. It is painted on paper and measures 26.9 cm in height and 22.2 cm in width.|The exact date of the album is unknown, but it is generally dated to the late 18th century.|The album currently contains 25 genre paintings, including A Village School and Korean Traditional Wrestling.|The album depicts everyday life in late Joseon, including work, education, leisure, and activities of people from various social groups.|The painting depicts a village school scene in which a young student sits crying in front of a teacher, while other students gather around them.|The crying student is shown with his back partly turned toward the viewer, while the surrounding students display different reactions. The exact reason for his tears is not established.|The teacher wears a square-shaped traditional hat called a banggeon and Confucian-style robes, distinguishing him from the students.|Some students appear amused by the crying child, while others watch the scene. Their varied facial expressions and gestures bring humor and liveliness to the painting.|Kim Hong-do arranged the figures in a roughly circular composition, directing attention toward the crying student and the teacher.|Detailed background elements are largely omitted to emphasize the figures’ expressions, postures, and movements. Kim Hong-do used swift and expressive brushstrokes to bring the scene to life.|The painting uses ink and light colors on paper. An educational heritage source describes Kim Hong-do’s use of iron-wire lines (cheolseonmyo) and nail-head-and-rat-tail lines (jeongduseomimyo) in depicting the figures.|In Joseon village schools, students commonly learned by reading aloud, memorizing, and repeatedly reciting classical texts. Instruction and assessment could be adapted to each student’s progress.|Kim Hong-do (1745–after 1806) was a leading painter of the Joseon dynasty who excelled in various genres, including landscape painting, bird-and-flower painting, and figure painting. He served as a court painter at the Royal Bureau of Painting (Dohwaseo) and employed a wide range of artistic styles, from refined court painting techniques to Western-influenced methods. His Album of Genre Paintings is among his representative works.|In many paintings in the album, Kim Hong-do minimized background details and emphasized the figures’ postures, gestures, and facial expressions to convey the atmosphere of everyday scenes.

title_en: Portrait of Kang Se-hwang, autograph version
key_facts: Kang Se-hwang (1713–1791) was a leading Joseon scholar-painter, calligrapher, writer, art critic, and government official.|The self-portrait is traditionally attributed to Kang Se-hwang and dated to 1782. Its inscription identifies him as 70 years old according to traditional Korean age reckoning and records the year of its creation.|The portrait is painted in colors on silk. The painted image measures 88.7 cm high and 51.0 cm wide, while the dimensions including its mounting are 150.0 by 61.5 cm.|The self-portrait is one of two paintings designated together as Treasure No. 590, Portrait of Kang Se-hwang. The other portrait is traditionally attributed to Yi Myeong-gi.|The portrait attributed to Yi Myeong-gi measures 145.5 by 94.0 cm and shows Kang in formal official robes. Both portraits are painted on silk and depict him seated in full-length compositions, with similarly angled faces and gazes directed to the right.|Self-portraits were extremely rare in Joseon portraiture, which primarily served commemorative and ritual purposes. Kang Se-hwang's and Yun Du-seo's self-portraits are notable surviving examples.|In a 2026 commentary, National Museum of Korea curator Kim Seung-ik emphasized the special significance of Kang's portrait as a fully realized self-portrait, contrasting it with Yun Du-seo's unfinished example.|Kang depicts himself wearing a black gauze official's hat (osamo) with informal scholar's robes, an unconventional combination under contemporary dress conventions.|According to official heritage commentary, the official's hat symbolizes Kang's achievements in government service, while his informal robe represents his attachment to scholarly life away from official duties.|The portrait contrasts a pale jade-blue robe with a red narrow belt (sejodae) decorated with gold pigment.|The face is rendered with detailed brush lines describing wrinkles and relatively strong shading along its sides. Official heritage commentary identifies Western-influenced techniques in this treatment.|The Korea Heritage Portal highlights the detailed depiction of finger joints in the two portraits as an important development in Joseon portrait painting.|The inscription at the top of the painting was composed by Kang and describes his appearance, learning, artistic identity, and aspirations.|In the inscription, Kang explains that his heart remains in the mountains and forests while his name is listed at court, expressing his dual identity as a government official and a scholar devoted to nature.|The inscription expresses pride in Kang's scholarship and artistic talent. It records his sobriquet Nojuk (露竹) and explicitly states that he painted the portrait and composed the inscription himself.|Kang devoted himself to scholarship and painting in Ansan before entering government service in 1773. He later supervised royal portrait production during King Jeongjo's reign and was a teacher and mentor of Kim Hong-do.|This self-portrait is distinct from another Portrait of Kang Se-hwang in the National Museum of Korea collection (Deoksu 3069), an anonymous portrait on paper measuring 50.9 by 31.5 cm. A glass-plate photographic record of that separate work is catalogued as Geonpan 17308.

unverified_facts: Researcher Lee Dong-cheon proposed in a 2013 Weekly Donga article that Kim Hong-do may have painted the 1782 portrait traditionally identified as Kang Se-hwang's self-portrait. His argument draws on historical writings, Kang's reported difficulty using his right arm in old age, and evidence that Kim Hong-do sometimes assisted Kang with painting. This remains an unconfirmed attribution hypothesis, not an established fact or the official attribution. The portrait's inscription explicitly claims that Kang painted it himself.

title_en: Endless Rivers and Mountains, by Yi In-mun
key_facts: Painted by Yi In-mun, a court painter of late Joseon whom the museum ranks alongside Kim Hong-do; he was good at landscapes, figures, and grapes rather than true-view landscapes or genre scenes.|On silk, 43.9 cm high and 856 cm long; designated a Treasure.|The museum calls it an unprecedented large work in Korean painting history: five pieces of silk were joined to depict an endless ideal landscape.|People living in harmony with unchanging nature appear throughout; tiny, finely drawn figures and varied, ornate texture strokes for the mountains create a dramatic view wherever the eye moves.|Yi In-mun reorganized the landscape as if looking down from a high place far away.|Seals reading 'Chusa' and 'Chusa jinjang' show that it once belonged to Kim Jeong-hui (1786-1856).

title_en: Painting of the Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn, by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: Official title: 김홍도 필 추성부도, by Kim Hong-do (1745-1806?), Joseon dynasty.|On paper, 214.7 cm by 55.8 cm; designated a Treasure.|The inscription on the painting is the text of the 'Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn' (Chuseongbu), whose narrator is Master Ouyang (Guyangja).|In the text, Master Ouyang, reading at night, hears a sound coming from the southwest and sends his servant boy to look; the boy says the stars and moon are bright and the sound is in the trees.|The narrator sighs that it is the sound of autumn; at the end the boy nods off, and only the chirping of insects is heard around the walls.

title_en: Woman Carrying a Baby on Her Back, by Shin Yun-bok
key_facts: Painted by Shin Yun-bok (1758?-after 1817), known for genre paintings of the romantic feelings of young men and women.|On paper, 23.3 cm by 24.8 cm.|A woman carrying a baby on her back is painted on a small sheet with no background.|At the lower right he wrote his pen name 'Hyewon' and stamped a square seal reading 'Wa-gan-un'.|The tall, slender young woman with a wide skirt and a large wig looks like a gisaeng (female entertainer), and the baby on her back conveys motherly love.|A long inscription by an unidentified writer, 'Buseol Geosa', compares the picture with paintings of beautiful women by the Tang Chinese painter Zhou Fang and notes that Zhou's paintings had no child on the back.
